title: Intangible Asset Amortization Rules, Methods, and Examples (September 2026)
summary: Learn how to amortize intangible assets in September 2026, from the straight-line formula and journal entries to Section 197 tax rules and GAAP vs. IFRS
body_markdown:
You record the purchase, but then what? For intangible assets, the answer is a scheduled amortization expense that flows through your income statement, builds up on your balance sheet, and gets added back on your cash flow statement. Understanding how all three connect makes the whole thing a lot less confusing than it looks at first glance.


**TLDR:**


- Amortize finite-life intangibles (patents, licenses, customer lists) straight-line using: Cost minus residual value, divided by useful life.
- Journal entries debit Amortization Expense and credit Accumulated Amortization, reducing net carrying value each period without touching original cost.
- Amortization reduces net income on the income statement, then gets added back on the cash flow statement since no cash leaves the business.
- Under IRC Section 197, most acquired intangibles amortize over **15 years** for tax purposes, regardless of book useful life, and goodwill amortization is tax deductible over that window.

## What Is Amortization of Intangible Assets


Amortization of intangible assets is the systematic process of expensing the cost of a finite-life intangible asset over the periods it generates economic benefit. Instead of recording the full purchase price as an expense on day one, you allocate a portion to each accounting period, matching the cost to the revenue it helps produce. The result is a recurring debit to Amortization Expense and a credit to Accumulated Amortization, reducing the asset's net carrying value on your balance sheet until it reaches zero.


Intangible assets lack physical form, so their value comes from legal rights, contractual relationships, or competitive advantages: a patent protecting a formula, a non-compete agreement restricting a former employee, or a customer list acquired in a business combination. GAAP requires you to amortize any intangible with a determinable useful life, using a method that reflects how the asset consumes value over time; straight-line is the default because most intangibles deliver a steady, predictable benefit across each period. Indefinite-life intangibles, like certain trademarks, skip amortization entirely and instead face annual impairment testing under ASC 350-30.


## Types of Intangible Assets Subject to Amortization


Intangible assets fall into two categories: identifiable and unidentifiable. Identifiable intangibles, like patents, customer lists, licenses, copyrights, and non-compete agreements, can be separated from the business and sold or transferred. Goodwill is the main unidentifiable intangible, since it only exists as part of a business combination.


Within identifiable intangibles, useful life determines whether amortization applies.


**Finite-life intangibles** (amortized over their useful life):


- Patents
- Customer lists
- Licenses
- Copyrights
- Non-compete agreements


**Indefinite-life intangibles** (not amortized):


- Certain trademarks
- Trade names


Under ASC 350-30, indefinite-life intangibles skip amortization and instead get tested for impairment at least once a year, or more often if events suggest the carrying value might not hold up.


## Determining the Useful Life of an Intangible Asset


Useful life is the period over which an intangible asset is expected to contribute economic benefit to the business. For a patent, that's often the remaining legal protection term (up to 20 years from the filing date), but the *economic* useful life may be shorter if the technology it covers is likely to be obsolete before the patent expires. A non-compete agreement tied to a three-year employment contract has a clear, contractually defined life; a customer list acquired in a business combination requires judgment about how long those relationships realistically generate revenue.


ASC 350-30 identifies several factors to weigh when estimating useful life: the expected use of the asset, any legal or contractual provisions that limit the period of use, the effects of obsolescence or changes in demand, and the useful lives of related assets. Where multiple factors apply, the shorter one generally controls. For example, a license might carry a 10-year term, but if the underlying software platform is expected to be replaced in five years, the five-year window drives the amortization schedule.


If none of those factors produces a reliable estimate, the asset is treated as having an indefinite life and removed from the amortization pool entirely, subject to annual impairment testing instead. Useful life is not a set-it-and-forget-it estimate: under GAAP, you review it whenever events or circumstances suggest the remaining period of benefit has changed, and revise the amortization rate prospectively if it has.


## Amortization of Intangible Assets Formula


Most intangible assets amortize using a straight-line formula:


Amortization Expense = (Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life in Periods


Cost covers the purchase price plus legal fees. Residual value is usually zero for intangibles. Useful life reflects the period the asset generates value.


A $100,000 patent amortized over 10 years produces $10,000 in annual expense, reducing carrying value each period.

## Methods of Amortization of Intangible Assets


Straight-line dominates because most intangibles deliver a steady, predictable benefit each period. GAAP requires it as the default, allowing alternatives only when a company shows a different consumption pattern.


- **Declining balance:** applies a fixed percentage to remaining book value, front-loading expense for assets like fast-fading tech.
- **Units-of-production:** ties amortization to output, such as a patent tied to units manufactured.
- **Sum-of-the-years-digits:** weights early periods heavier, less common but permitted.


## Amortization of Intangible Assets: Worked Examples


A customer list acquired for $60,000 in a business combination, with a 5 year useful life, amortizes at $12,000 per year under the straight line method.


A software license bought for $24,000 with a 4 year term amortizes at $500 monthly, or $6,000 annually, until book value hits zero. The formula holds steady: divide the amortizable cost by the useful life, then post that amount each period.


## Journal Entry for Amortization of Intangible Assets


The standard journal entry for amortizing an intangible asset debits Amortization Expense and credits Accumulated Amortization. This mirrors the[depreciation journal entry](https://doublehq.com/blog/depreciation-journal-entry-guide/) contra-asset treatment: the asset account keeps its original cost, while a separate accumulated balance grows each period to reduce the carrying value shown on the balance sheet.


Take a non-compete agreement acquired for $18,000 with a 3 year useful life. Straight-line amortization posts $6,000 per year, or $500 per month if the close runs monthly.


Amortization Expense flows to the income statement as an operating expense, reducing net income for the period. Like an[accrued expenses journal entry](https://doublehq.com/blog/accrued-expenses-journal-entry/) , the debit-credit pattern here follows the same matching principle. Accumulated Amortization sits on the balance sheet as a contra-asset, netted against the non-compete agreement's original cost to show a carrying value of $12,000 after year one. The same debit-credit pattern applies whether you're recording a patent amortization journal entry, a license, or any other finite-life intangible: only the account name and dollar figures change.


## Amortization of Intangible Assets on Financial Statements


Amortization touches all three statements, but each treats it differently based on what it measures.


On the income statement, amortization expense sits inside operating expenses, usually folded into SG&A, and tracking those period-over-period changes is where[variance accounting](https://doublehq.com/blog/variance-accounting-guide/) and[flux analysis](https://doublehq.com/blog/flux-analysis-explained-complete-guide/) matter, though some companies embed it in COGS when the intangible directly supports production, like a manufacturing patent. Either placement reduces operating income and net income for the period, even though no cash changes hands.


On the balance sheet, amortization never touches the intangible asset's original cost. Instead, it builds up in Accumulated Amortization, a contra-asset account netted against the gross carrying value to show what's left. A patent recorded at $100,000 with $30,000 of accumulated amortization shows a $70,000 net carrying value, with both figures often disclosed separately in a[rollforward in accounting](https://doublehq.com/blog/rollforward-in-accounting-guide/) schedule.


The cash flow statement is where amortization gets added back. Since it reduced net income without any cash leaving the business, the indirect-method cash flow statement adds amortization expense back to net income in operating activities. This keeps cash flow from operations tied to actual cash movement, not the accounting allocation of an already-paid cost.


## Amortization vs. Depreciation of Intangible Assets


Amortization and depreciation solve the same problem: matching an asset's cost to the periods it benefits, instead of expensing the full amount on day one, and confirming those balances is a core step in[general ledger reconciliation](https://doublehq.com/blog/general-ledger-reconciliation/) . Depreciation applies to physical assets like buildings, machinery, and vehicles, anything with physical form that wears down. Amortization applies to intangible assets, the patents, licenses, and customer relationships that have no physical presence but still lose value.


That distinction answers whether intangible assets get amortization or depreciation. The answer depends on physical form, not value. A $2 million patent amortizes. A $2 million factory depreciates. Both reduce net income gradually through a contra-asset account, but the asset type determines the term.


Method selection tends to split along the same line. Intangible assets usually amortize on a straight-line basis with no salvage value, since a secondhand market rarely exists for a partially used trademark or customer list. Physical assets more often use accelerated methods like double-declining balance, reflecting how equipment loses more usefulness early on and often retains resale or scrap value at the end.


Residual value follows this logic too. For intangibles, residual value is assumed to be zero unless a third party has already committed, in writing, to purchase the asset at the end of its useful life. That bar is high, which is why nearly every amortization schedule assumes the full cost gets written off to nothing.


## Amortization and Impairment of Intangible Assets


Amortization runs on a set schedule. Impairment strikes without warning when something breaks, a patent loses relevance, a customer relationship dies, a trade name tied to an underperforming unit.


Finite-life intangibles use a two-step ASC 360-10 test: compare carrying value to undiscounted cash flows, then measure loss against fair value if needed. Teams still managing accruals manually in Excel face added risk when impairment flags arise mid-period. Indefinite-life intangibles skip straight to a one-step ASC 350-30 fair-value test. Impairment losses post as a separate income statement line and cannot be reversed under US GAAP.


## Goodwill Amortization: GAAP Rules and the Private Company Alternative


Under US GAAP, public companies do not amortize goodwill. ASC 350-20 requires an annual impairment test comparing each reporting unit's fair value to its carrying value, a review typically scheduled as part of the[month-end close process](https://doublehq.com/blog/month-end-close-process-guide/) , with any shortfall posted as a one-time, non-reversible charge to the income statement.


Private companies have a different path. Under ASU 2014-02, they may amortize goodwill straight-line over 10 years or less, trading yearly fair value testing for a fixed expense each period. This is the[private company goodwill accounting alternative](https://legalclarity.org/amortization-of-goodwill-for-accounting-and-tax/) , where testing then triggers only on specific events, at the entity level.


## Tax Amortization of Intangible Assets: Section 197 and the 15-Year Rule


Tax rules for intangibles follow a separate track from GAAP. Under[IRC Section 197](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/intangibles) , most acquired intangibles amortize straight-line over 15 years, regardless of actual useful life, which is worth including in any[month-end close checklist](https://doublehq.com/blog/month-end-close-checklist/) for businesses with acquired intangibles. According to the IRS, this applies to intangibles acquired after August 10, 1993, held in a trade or business, including goodwill, customer lists, and trademarks. Goodwill amortization is tax deductible over that 15-year window. Taxpayers report the deduction on Form 4562.


## GAAP vs. IFRS: Key Differences in Amortization of Intangible Assets


GAAP and IFRS share the same core mechanics for amortizing intangible assets, but they split on three judgment calls. GAAP expenses research and development as incurred; IAS 38 records development costs as an asset once technical feasibility is proven. GAAP holds intangibles at cost with no upward revaluation; IFRS permits fair value revaluation for assets with active markets. IAS 38 requires annual useful life reviews; GAAP reviews only after a triggering event. Tech, pharma, and media see the largest earnings swings from these gaps.
